conflicts.note: The likely reality is a running change — early-production 165.024s carried over batons from the late 165.014, with sword hands becoming standard during the run — but sources do not pin down the exact transition. Be cautious about treating sword hands as universally correct for every 165.024.
positions: Hairspring's 'Big Triangle' write-up describes the 165.024 as introducing the sword handset alongside the lyre-lug case and graduated bezel — i.e. sword hands are the canonical 165.024 handset.
Hairspring's fourth 165.024 find notes 'some had sword hands, though this '63 watch does not,' implying a baton-handed early-production variant and/or that not all 165.024s carry sword hands.

conflicts.note: The case is typically described at 42mm including bezel; the 41mm figure likely reflects a different measuring point. Worth flagging rather than asserting a single figure.
positions: Most editorial sources and Hodinkee Shop listings cite the 165.024 case as 42mm.
Two Hodinkee Shop listings give the diameter as 41mm with a 13mm thickness.

consensus.claim: The Seamaster 300 165.024 succeeded the straight-lug 2913 (1957) and the transitional references 14755 and 165.014, introducing a 42mm twisted lyre-lug case, simplified fully-graduated bakelite bezel, tritium (replacing radium), and a sword handset.

The 165.024 case was produced by two external casemakers — initially Huguenin Frères (HF) and later Centrale Boîtes (CB) — identifiable by stamps inside the caseback. The same two suppliers also made Speedmaster cases of the period.
The 165.024 was rated to 200m water resistance, with casebacks engraved 'Certified High Pressure Waterproof' beside the Seamaster Hippocampus.
The watch was driven by Omega's self-winding calibre 550/552 family; period-correct examples are typically delivered on the flat-link Omega 1039 bracelet with 516 end links.

The British MoD took delivery of mil-spec Seamaster 300s between 1967 and 1971, issued to both Royal Navy and British Army; military examples differ from civilian 165.024s in three ways — a circled T on the dial (with some early genuine examples lacking it), fixed (welded) springbars for NATO-only fitment, and caseback engravings ('0552' prefix for Royal Navy, 'W10' for Army).
The 165.024 was also used by other militaries — issued examples are documented for the Israeli Defence Forces (including Air Force pilots) with Extracts of Archive confirming Israeli delivery.

Originality is the central market problem for the 165.024: in the early 2000s, Omega-authorised Australian service centre WatchCo discovered a cache of original surplus Seamaster 300 parts and assembled them into complete watches sold as 'NOS' Seamasters; the components themselves are genuine Omega parts, but the resulting watches are not period-original.

The 42mm case was unusually large for a 1960s dive watch and reads as modern on the wrist; design cues — fully-lumed bakelite bezel, sword hands and big triangle at 12 — have been reused on modern Omega divers (notably the 2254.50 and the 2019 SMP 300M Bond editions).

Bakelite bezel inserts on the 165.024 are fragile and frequently cracked — most often radiating from the 30-minute area — so an uncracked, fully-lumed bezel with even patina is a key originality marker.
Values for honest, unmolested 165.024s rose sharply during 2019–2023; one source frames it as moving from around USD 5,000 five years prior to roughly three to four times that for great examples.

Hairspring's writers explicitly compare the 165.024's design pedigree and tool-watch credentials to the Rolex Submariner 5513 and the vintage Blancpain Fifty Fathoms, attributing its lower historical price to longer/larger production rather than to design or quality.

The transitional 165.014 (c.1962–64) retains the 2913's straight-lug case and bakelite bezel but updates the dial, handset and reference numbering system; late-production 165.014s adopted sword hands, briefly anticipating the 165.024 handset.

The modern Seamaster Diver 300M is a separate 1993 model line (ref. 2541/2531 onward) that revived the Seamaster name as a professional diver; it shares the design language of a wave-textured dial, lyre lugs and helium-escape valve and became the on-screen watch of James Bond from 1995's GoldenEye onward.

The 1995 Omega/Bond partnership was driven initially by costume designer Lindy Hemming, not by a paid product-placement deal; Omega supplied watches free of charge for GoldenEye, and the broader commercial partnership developed afterwards.

marks.explanation: 165.024 cases were supplied by Huguenin Frères (HF, earlier production) and Centrale Boîtes (CB, later). The inside of the caseback is stamped 'HF' or 'CB' — a quick originality cross-check.
marks.name: Casemaker stamp inside caseback

marks.explanation: Outside caseback carries the Seamaster Hippocampus plus 'Certified High Pressure Waterproof'; military versions instead bear unit-specific engravings beginning with 0552 (Royal Navy) or W10 (Army).
marks.name: Caseback engraving

marks.explanation: The full-lume bakelite insert is fragile and prone to hairline cracks (often near 30); an intact, unrelumed bezel with patina matching the dial is a strong originality indicator and a meaningful value driver.
marks.name: Bakelite bezel condition

marks.explanation: Genuine, period-original watches typically show consistent tritium aging across dial plots, hands and bezel numerals; mismatches are a red flag for parts swapping or WatchCo assembly. Note that hands often age slightly lighter than dial lume — documented as a common SM300 trait, not necessarily a problem.
marks.name: Tritium patina match across dial, hands and bezel

marks.explanation: Watches assembled in the early 2000s from genuine surplus parts by the Australian service centre WatchCo are not period-original. Extract of Archive, casemaker stamp, bracelet/end-link correctness and overall component coherence are the practical filters.
marks.name: WatchCo assembly check

marks.explanation: Period-correct delivery is the Omega 1039 flat-link bracelet with 516 end links; clasp date stamps (e.g. '2 67', '1 69') should sit close to the production year on the Extract.
marks.name: Bracelet and end links

marks.explanation: Mil-spec dials carry a small circled T marking tritium content; some early genuine MoD examples lack it, so absence alone does not disqualify a military watch — the caseback engraving and fixed springbars are the harder evidence.
marks.name: Military 'circled T' dial

marks.explanation: MoD-issued 165.024s have welded/fixed springbars for NATO strap use only — a structural give-away that the watch was built to military specification.
marks.name: Fixed springbars

marks.explanation: Self-winding Omega calibres 550 and 552 are correct for the 165.024 production span; movement number and Extract of Archive should align with the case generation.
marks.name: Calibre 550 / 552

model_context: The Omega Seamaster 300 (ref. 165.024) sits within Omega's professional tool-watch line, introduced in 1957 as a purpose-built diver alongside the Speedmaster (chronograph) and Railmaster (anti-magnetic) — the so-called 'professional trilogy.' The 165.024, produced from roughly 1962/64 through 1969, is the third-generation Seamaster 300, characterised by a 42mm twisted lyre-lug case, fully graduated bakelite bezel, no-date matte black dial, sword handset and tritium lume. It supplanted the straight-lug 2913 (1957) and the transitional 14755 / 165.014 (1960–64). Demand for the watch came from genuine professional use — it was commissioned by the British MoD and issued to Royal Navy divers, Royal Marines and the British Army between 1967 and 1971, with a small but real footprint among other militaries (notably the Israeli Defence Forces). On the civilian side, it competed directly with the Rolex Submariner and Blancpain Fifty Fathoms as a 200m-rated tool diver, but production volumes and length-of-run meant it has historically traded for less than either. The lineage is also the foundation of Omega's modern Seamaster Diver 300M (Pierce Brosnan/Daniel Craig-era Bond watch) introduced in 1993 — a separate, modern line that shares the name and a broad design language but no direct case parts. The 165.024's appeal today is grounded in originality scarcity (heavily affected by WatchCo-era parts assembly), military provenance, and a design considered by many to be Omega's most fully resolved dive watch.

module_candidates.rationale: The 1967–71 British military 165.024 deserves its own page: dial T-circle, fixed springbars, RN/Army caseback prefixes, distribution irregularities and named-veteran provenance examples all warrant separate, focused treatment without crowding the civilian reference page.

module_candidates.rationale: Sources repeatedly conflate the vintage Seamaster 300 with the modern SMP 300M. A clean, separate module covering the 1993 2541/2531, the Brosnan/Craig Bond lineage, and the 2018 ceramic generation would prevent that conflation here.

Explicitly designed with 165.024 cues (sword hands, big triangle); a sibling page makes the lineage visible and gives readers a modern lateral option to the vintage 300.

source_contributions.unique_contribution: Detailed timeline of the transitional 165.014 (1962–64), the change from radium to tritium, and the late-production 165.014 sword-hand variant — the bridge piece between the 2913 and 165.024.

Provenance story for an Israeli Air Force–issued 165.014 awarded to an F-4E Phantom pilot in 1966, with archive extract confirming Israeli delivery — and broader context on Omega/Tudor as the dominant IDF watch suppliers of the period.

The clearest single account of British MoD-issued 165.024s: 1967–1971 delivery window, circled-T dial, fixed springbars, and the W10 (Army) / 0552 (RN) caseback prefixes, plus a real-named provenance from a 15/19th King's Royal Hussars Chieftain tank Regimental Quartermaster.
Sets out the 'Big Triangle' nickname, summarises the design transition from 2913/165.014 to 165.024, and notes the HF/CB casemaker split.

Origin and mechanics of the WatchCo phenomenon — surplus original Omega parts assembled in Australia in the early 2000s and retailed as NOS Seamasters — and the central role this plays in 165.024 originality assessment.
Market trajectory: a five-year price climb from roughly USD 5K to 3–4× that, and a direct lateral comparison to the Rolex 5513 and vintage Fifty Fathoms.

A detailed single-family ownership story — 1967 purchase in South Korea by a US Army second lieutenant for USD 100 (roughly a third of his monthly pay) — illustrating the watch's role as a working serviceman's daily.
Period-specific specs and casing details for a 1967 HF-cased 165.024 (calibre 550, 42mm × 14mm, plexi crystal) plus the explicit 'Certified High Pressure Waterproof' caseback wording.
Confirms a 1968 CB-cased example delivered to Australia, with calibre 552 and an HF→CB transition timing data point.
Detailed condition language for an exceptional 1967 165.024 on its original 1039/516 bracelet, including the typical handset-vs-dial lume aging differential noted as common to SM300s.
Documents a 1967 CB-cased 165.024 delivered to Mexico, with the clasp dated 1/69 and a note on color-corrected hand lume — useful as a transparency-of-disclosure benchmark.
Explicitly identifies the sword-hand 2254.50 SMP as borrowing the sword hands and big-triangle 12 marker from the 165.024, tying the modern SMP lineage to the vintage 300 visually.
Foundational history of the 1993 Seamaster Diver 300M ref. 2541/2531, the introduction of the wave dial, and the original 1990s retail-vs-secondhand pricing.
Comprehensive chronology of Omega/Bond limited editions from 2002 (Die Another Day) onward — useful for separating the SMP 300M Bond line from the vintage Seamaster 300.
Lindy Hemming's 1995 GoldenEye decision-making, including her stated rationale for choosing Omega over Rolex and the fact that watches were initially supplied free, not as paid product placement.
The Rolex-as-Bond counter-position, useful for framing why the modern SMP is often discussed in opposition to a vintage tool-diver heritage.

stories.title: Issued to a Royal Hussars tank officer
stories.why: A real-named British Army provenance — a Regimental Quartermaster of the 15/19th King's Royal Hussars who served in Germany, Cyprus and Northern Ireland in a Chieftain main battle tank from 1960–82 — wearing a Royal Navy-engraved (0552) 165.024. Concretely illustrates the loose MoD distribution and the watch's actual service use.

stories.title: Awarded to an Israeli Air Force F-4E Phantom pilot, 1966
stories.why: A 165.014 awarded by the IDF on graduation from training, with extract confirming Israeli delivery. Demonstrates that Omega's military adoption extended beyond the British MoD and gives a vivid mid-1960s Middle East context to the early Seamaster 300 references.

stories.title: USD 100 in South Korea, 1967 — two wrists, one family
stories.why: A second lieutenant bought the 165.024 new at a US Army base in South Korea for USD 100 — roughly a third of his monthly pay — wore it for twenty years, gave it to his teenage son, took it back when it was treated carelessly, wore it another twenty years, then re-gifted it. A grounded counter-narrative to the watch-as-investment framing.

stories.title: WatchCo and the surplus-parts problem
stories.why: In the early 2000s an Omega-authorised Australian service centre, WatchCo, discovered a cache of original Seamaster 300 parts and assembled them into 'NOS' Seamasters. Because the components themselves are genuine Omega, these watches sit in an ambiguous zone — the defining authenticity question for any 165.024 buyer today.
